name: Spherical Coordinates (Introduction)
description: Describing points on a sphere using distance, angle around, and angle up/down.

content.overview: Think about how you'd pin down any spot on Earth: how far from the center of the planet, what longitude, what latitude. That's it—you've just described spherical coordinates, the system built for anything shaped like a globe. {{viz:diagram-01}}
content.explanation:
Spherical coordinates are the natural choice for spheres and for anything that radiates outward from a single point. A point is written as (r, θ, φ):
- r = distance from the center
- θ = the azimuthal angle—your horizontal swing, basically longitude
- φ = the polar angle—your vertical tilt, basically latitude (measured down from the top) {{viz:diagram-02}}

**Where you've actually seen this:** GPS. Every satellite sits at some distance from Earth's center, swung to some angle east-west, and tilted to some angle north-south. That's spherical coordinates quietly running in the background of your phone. {{viz:anim-01}}

**Where physics leans on it:** electrons buzzing around a nucleus, planets orbiting the sun, light spilling out from a bulb in every direction—anywhere there's an orbit or something radiating outward, spherical coordinates are the natural fit. {{viz:chart-01}}

Side by side:
- **Cartesian** (x, y, z): "go 3 right, 2 forward, 4 up"
- **Spherical** (r, θ, φ): "go 5 units out, swing to this compass direction, tilt up by this angle"

Spherical coordinates click whenever you've got spherical symmetry—when a system looks the same in every direction from its center, like an atom or a star.

Honestly, it's just polar coordinates that leveled up: instead of a flat circle, you're now wrapping around a full sphere, so you pick up one extra angle to describe the tilt.
keyPoints: Spherical = (r, θ, φ) for describing points in 3D
r = distance from the origin (the center)
θ = azimuthal angle—your horizontal swing, like longitude
φ = polar angle—your vertical tilt, like latitude
The go-to system for orbits, atoms, and radiation
Feels natural any time a system has spherical symmetry
content.whyItMatters: Atoms, planets, radiating light—so much of physics has this spherical symmetry baked in, and spherical coordinates let you work with that shape instead of fighting it. What looks like a tangled mess in (x, y, z) often turns clean and simple the moment you switch to (r, θ, φ).
